topic: Mobile one-handed UX for list/checklist apps: thumb reach, touch target size and spacing, bottom-anchored controls, handedness, accidental-tap prevention, undo, progress and state feedback, micro-interaction timing

findings.claim: Hoober 2013 grip study: most people touching a phone use one hand, and the thumb does the work.
findings.detail: Hoober and colleagues logged 1,333 observations of people using mobile devices in public places; 780 were touching the screen. Among those, one-handed grip was 49%, cradled (one hand holds, other hand taps) 36%, two-handed 15%. The widely repeated '75% thumb' figure comes from secondary sources and is not confirmed in the column text I could reach. The column's editor note says Hoober later updated his guidelines (see 'Design for Fingers, Touch, and People', 2017), so the 2013 numbers are dated.

findings.claim: Handedness split: among one-handed users the right thumb was on screen about 67% of the time and the left thumb about 33%.
findings.detail: Reported by Addy Osmani's summary and a second blog quoting Hoober's breakdown; the original UXmatters text was not retrievable here. Implication: roughly one in three one-handed users is on the left thumb, so a right-anchored layout (the app's deliberate choice) should be a default with a mirror option, not the only mode.

findings.claim: The 'thumb zone' concept originates with Hoober; the comfortable zone mirrors for left-handed users and does not grow with screen size.
findings.detail: Hoober coined the Thumb Zone (Designing Mobile Interfaces). Secondary summaries say the natural zone is the bottom-center/bottom-side area, side-mid screen needs a stretch, and far top corners are hardest. Because thumbs do not scale with phones, the easy area stays about the same on large screens, so top areas get worse as screens grow. The three-color map (green/yellow/red) is a secondary-source depiction, not Hoober's own figure.

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed model of the thumb's functional reach area exists (CHI 2014).
findings.detail: Bergstrom-Lehtovirta and Oulasvirta derive a quadratic model of the thumb's reachable area from kinematics, with surface size, hand size and index-finger position on the back of the device as inputs, validated on thumb-motion trajectories from 20 participants. Takeaway: reach is a function of hand size and grip, so a fixed pixel 'safe zone' is an approximation; keep the primary controls in the lower portion and avoid requiring the far opposite (left) corner.

findings.claim: Parhi, Karlson and Bederson (MobileHCI 2006): 9.2 mm (discrete targets) and 9.6 mm (serial targets) are large enough for one-handed thumb use.
findings.detail: Phase 1 tested single targets such as buttons and checkboxes, phase 2 sequential tasks such as text entry. Speed improved as targets grew; error rates showed no significant difference at 9.6 mm or more for discrete tasks and 7.7 mm or more for serial tasks. Target position on screen was varied. NN/g cites this work for a 1 cm x 1 cm minimum, stressed as a physical measurement not a pixel count, and notes MIT Touch Lab data that fingertips are 1.6-2 cm wide.

findings.claim: Apple: touch targets should be at least 44 x 44 points (60 x 60 pt on visionOS).
findings.detail: Apple's Buttons HIG is quoted as 'a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt' and the older Apple UI Design Dos and Don'ts page says 'Create controls that measure at least 44 points x 44 points so they can be accurately tapped with a finger.' Points are density-independent, comparable to CSS px on the web. I saw these through search excerpts and a developer-forum quote, not by reading the Apple page in full.

findings.claim: Google/Material/Android: targets at least 48 x 48 dp (about 9 mm) with at least 8 dp between them; the visible glyph may be smaller than the hit area.
findings.detail: Google's Android accessibility help says a 24 dp icon with padding still counts as a 48 dp target. Compose Checkbox/Switch add padding to reach 48 dp. Small closely packed targets cannot always be enlarged without overlap, so spacing becomes the constraint.

findings.claim: Web tooling uses 48 x 48 CSS px with about 8 px spacing as the practical target.
findings.detail: Lighthouse flags a tap target only if it is smaller than 48x48 px AND at least 25% of the area within 48 px of its centre overlaps another target; targets at 48x48 px never fail. Fixes: add padding (so icon look is unchanged) or margin; '8 px between tap targets is a good starting point' but not always enough for very small targets. web.dev states 48 px corresponds to around 9 mm on a site with a proper mobile viewport.

findings.claim: WCAG 2.2 sets two target-size levels: 2.5.8 (AA) minimum 24 x 24 CSS px; 2.5.5 (AAA) enhanced 44 x 44 CSS px.
findings.detail: 2.5.8 has exceptions for spacing (a 24 px circle centred on an undersized target must not intersect another target), equivalent alternatives, inline links and essential cases. The 24 px floor is a legal minimum, not a one-handed usability target. Some secondary pages mislabel 2.5.8 as a WCAG 2.1 criterion; it is new in 2.2.

findings.claim: Older physical-size guidance: Microsoft 9 mm ideal / 7 mm fallback; Hoober slide deck 6 mm min, 8 mm preferred, 15 mm max, with spacing guidance of 8 mm min / 10 mm preferred measured from centre.
findings.detail: Microsoft's archived Windows Phone guide says 9 mm square is ideal across its touch platforms, 7 mm only when space is tight; a 2 mm/8 px minimum gap is quoted second-hand. Hoober's deck lists min 17 pt / 6 mm, preferred 23 pt / 8 mm, max 43 pt / 15 mm. The sources converge on roughly 7-10 mm as the working band, with 9-10 mm best for thumbs.

findings.claim: Hoober's slide-deck target numbers (6/8/15 mm; 8/10 mm spacing) come from a SlideShare deck, not a primary article.
findings.detail: The deck lists min 17 pt / 6 mm, preferred 23 pt / 8 mm, max 43 pt / 15 mm, with centre-measured interference spacing min 23 pt / 8 mm, preferred 28 pt / 10 mm. The newer UXmatters series ('Design for Fingers, Touch, and People', Parts 1-3, 2017) was not retrievable and may state different values.

findings.claim: Fitts's law: bigger and closer is faster, but the 'magic edge' advantage does not transfer to touch, and big/close destructive actions are easy to hit by accident.
findings.detail: Movement time depends on distance and target size. The edge/corner 'infinite target' argument comes from mouse cursors that stop at the screen edge; on touch the user's hand position is unknown and thumb reach dominates. Corollary for this app: make the tick row large, but keep Close/Done visually and spatially separated from ticks.

findings.claim: Bottom-placed controls are standard industrial-design logic (content top, controls bottom), but fixed-position web UI at the bottom is unreliable in mobile browsers.
findings.detail: Josh Clark's Designing for Touch argues for controls at the bottom within thumb sweep and cautions that position:fixed pinned navigation on the mobile web has reliability problems. Relevant to a no-scroll fixed-viewport app: use dynamic viewport units and safe-area insets rather than assuming a stable viewport.

findings.claim: Pointer cancellation (WCAG 2.5.2, Level A): activate on the up-event so a user can slide off to abort.
findings.detail: Sufficient ways include: down-event not used to execute the function, or an abort/undo mechanism, or the up-event reverses the down-event. Native controls (button, input) behave correctly by default (technique G212). On touch, up-event activation only fires if the finger lifts within the target boundary.

findings.claim: Dragging needs a non-drag alternative (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7, Level AA).
findings.detail: Any function operated by dragging must also work with a single pointer without dragging (tap/click), unless dragging is essential. For reorderable lists the standard fix is visible up/down buttons or a 'Move to position' menu; drag may remain as an enhancement. Also helps users with tremor and users in unstable environments (walking, transit).

findings.claim: Prefer undo over 'Are you sure?' confirmation for reversible actions.
findings.detail: Aza Raskin (A List Apart, 2007): users form habits and click through warnings, so a warning is the wrong tool when the action is reversible; give undo instead. Secondary UX sources agree: dialog fatigue sets in when confirmations are routine, so reserve confirmations for high-consequence/irreversible actions, displace the confirm button from where the trigger sat, and consider a short delay to defeat accidental double-taps. Shake-to-undo should not be the only path (low discoverability).

findings.claim: Undo windows in the wild: Gmail Undo Send defaults to 5 s, configurable to 10, 20 or 30 s; design systems put undo toasts at about 5 s (no action) and 10 s (with action).
findings.detail: Gmail's mechanism holds the message for the period rather than recalling it. One design system (customer.io) specifies snackbars persist 5 s without an action and 10 s with an action; Acorn says an action snackbar may be 'slightly longer'. Angular Material warns against timed snackbars with actions because screen-reader users may need longer (a WCAG 2.2.1 timing concern). Older Android snackbar library defaults were 2 s short / 3.5 s long, which are library values, not Material spec.

findings.claim: Response-time limits: 0.1 s feels instantaneous, 1 s keeps flow of thought, 10 s is the attention limit.
findings.detail: Nielsen (from Miller 1968): at 100 ms the outcome feels caused by the user and no special feedback is needed beyond showing the result; around 1 s users notice the delay but keep their train of thought; at 10 s attention drifts and a progress indicator with expected completion is needed.

findings.claim: Material 2 motion durations: typical mobile transition about 300 ms; entering 225 ms; leaving 195 ms; large/full-screen 375 ms; over 400 ms feels too slow; tablet about +30%, wearable about -30%.
findings.detail: Leaving elements can be shorter because they need less attention; short travel distances and minor surface changes get shorter durations. This is the official archived Material 2 spec page.

findings.claim: Animation rule of thumb: 100-500 ms total, justify anything over 300 ms; Material 3 tokens start at 50 ms with an emphasized easing of cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1).
findings.detail: The 100-500 ms range is attributed to NN/g by secondary blogs (NN/g page not retrieved). The MD3 token values (short1 50 ms, medium1 250 ms, long1 450 ms, emphasized cubic-bezier(0.2,0.0,0,1)) come from a third-party summary and a GitHub issue, not m3.material.io directly.

findings.claim: Responsiveness budget on the web: Interaction to Next Paint of 200 ms or less is 'good' (75th percentile); over 500 ms is poor.
findings.detail: This is Google's Core Web Vitals threshold for the delay from input to next frame. For a tick tap the visual change should land far inside this, ideally in the same frame as the 100 ms 'instant' limit.

findings.claim: Long-press threshold on Android is 400 ms (changed from 500 ms in AOSP to match the system setting).
findings.detail: Relevant for choosing a long-press-to-drag or long-press-for-detail delay so it does not feel different from the OS. Older Android source still shows 500 ms. iOS: no verified system default found; Apple does not expose the user's Haptic Touch speed to apps.

findings.claim: Progress psychology: visible progress toward a goal increases completion (endowed-progress and goal-gradient effects).
findings.detail: Nunes and Drèze (2006) car-wash loyalty cards: cards pre-stamped with 2 stamps had 34% redemption vs 19% for unendowed cards. Kivetz, Urminsky and Zheng (2006) found a sense of advancement accelerates goal completion; effort rises as psychological distance to the goal shrinks. These are consumer-loyalty field experiments, so effect sizes for a checklist app are unknown. A UX reading is to emphasise what remains rather than only what is done.

findings.claim: Determinate-progress timing guidance from a vendor design system: show an indicator after about 1 s; use determinate bars when duration is known or over 10 s.
findings.detail: This is Astro UX (a design system), not NN/g. It mirrors the Nielsen 1 s / 10 s limits. A checklist run is a user-paced process with a known total (n items), which is the ideal case for a determinate 'x of n' indicator rather than a spinner.

findings.claim: State feedback must not rely on color alone (WCAG 1.4.1) and must be exposed programmatically (4.1.2).
findings.detail: For done/pending/skipped, give each state a distinct shape or text cue (for example empty box, check mark, dash or slash, plus text such as 'Skipped') in addition to color, and expose state to assistive tech via name/role/value. A legend explaining colors does not satisfy 1.4.1.

findings.claim: Vibration API is Android-only; iOS Safari and all iOS browsers do not support navigator.vibrate.
findings.detail: Chrome requires a user gesture (Chrome 60+). Feature-detect with 'vibrate' in navigator; calls are no-ops where unsupported. Haptic confirmation therefore cannot be relied on; tick sound and spoken confirmation (already in the app) and a strong visual change must carry the feedback on iPhone.

findings.claim: ADHD-oriented design advice found is practitioner opinion, not rigorous research.
findings.detail: Recurring ideas: one primary action per screen, immediate feedback on completion, break work into small steps, show only the current task, visible progress for time blindness. Claims like 'ADHD templates raise completion by up to 50%' cite no study. Gamification effects are contested; test with neurodivergent users.

recommendations: Define target sizes as design-independent tokens, shared by all three skins: --hit-min: 48px (equals 48dp and about 9 mm per Google/web.dev, above Apple's 44 pt and Parhi 2006's 9.2-9.6 mm), --hit-gap: 8px minimum between adjacent targets. Make the Airplane (dense) skin shrink the visible glyph, never the hit area.

Run screen: make the entire item row the tap target, not only the tick box. Use row min-height about 56px (comfortably above 48) with a visible tick box of 28-32px on the right; row-to-row gap at least 8px. Rows that are only 48px high with no gap are borderline given Lighthouse's 25 percent overlap rule.

Keep primary actions (Close/Done, Save, + New) in the bottom-right band, but respect safe areas: padding-bottom/right with env(safe-area-inset-*) so the home-indicator and gesture-nav zones are not part of the hit area. Keep secondary actions (Cancel, Questions) in the same bottom row, within one thumb sweep of Save, rather than at the top-left.

Ship a Left-handed layout switch in Settings (default Right, as the user wants). Roughly 33 percent of one-handed users use the left thumb (Hoober via Osmani). Implement with a data-hand attribute that flips inline direction so checkmarks, stack anchor and primary buttons mirror together.

Separate dangerous from frequent: ticks are the highest-frequency action, so keep Close/Done at least one full target (48px plus gap) away from the topmost/bottommost tick row, and never place a destructive action where the last tap landed. Mid-run Close with unchecked items should offer a lightweight state ('3 of 8 done, keep going / close anyway') rather than a generic dialog.

Make ticking self-reversible instead of confirming it: tapping a done row again unticks it, and the whole toggle is instant. For irreversible or bulk actions (delete checklist, reset run, delete point) use an Undo toast, not 'Are you sure?' (Raskin). Suggested windows: 5 s for simple actions, 8-10 s when the toast has an Undo action (Gmail 5 s default; design systems 5/10 s). Pause the countdown on touch/focus and do not auto-dismiss under assistive tech, to respect WCAG 2.2.1.

Activate on click/pointerup, not pointerdown, so a finger can slide off to cancel (WCAG 2.5.2). Use native button/input elements or equivalent. Optionally ignore taps whose pointerdown-to-up movement exceeds a small slop (about 8-10 px) so a scroll attempt in the references page does not trigger a toggle.

Feedback timing budget for micro-interactions: pressed state visible in the same frame (0-50 ms, instant in, no transition); tick/check state change completes visually in 120-200 ms; row reorder/entry 200-250 ms; screen transitions about 225 ms in / 195 ms out, 300 ms ceiling (Material 2: 300 typical, 375 large, over 400 feels slow); nothing decorative over 500 ms. Audio and speech confirmation should be triggered synchronously from the same user gesture (needed to unlock audio on iOS), targeting under 100 ms perceived delay.

prefers-reduced-motion: keep the instant state change and the color/shape change, drop movement and checkmark drawing; replace animated progress with a stepped fill. Do not rely on motion alone to convey a state change.

Progress indicator: show a determinate 'x of n' count (text) plus a segmented bar with one segment per item, near the thumb zone (bottom-right) rather than the top. Phrase it around what remains ('5 left') as well as what is done, since the goal-gradient effect is about distance to goal. Count 'required' items separately so Done can show 'all required done'. Do not fake or pre-fill progress (the endowed-progress trick would misrepresent a checklist).

Three item states with redundant cues, in every skin: pending = empty box; done = check mark; skipped = dash/slash plus the text 'Skipped'. Expose via accessible names or aria-checked/aria-label text. Color may differ per skin, but the shape/text cue must not.

Drag-to-reorder in the editor: give each point a drag handle of at least 48px and also an accessible non-drag path (up/down buttons or a 'Move to position' action) to satisfy WCAG 2.5.7. If using long-press to start a drag, use about 400 ms to match Android's system long-press, with a visible lift (scale/shadow) at the moment it arms.

Use haptics only as a progressive enhancement (navigator.vibrate on Android with a short 10-20 ms pulse, feature-detected); iOS Safari ignores it, so sound/speech and visual change must be sufficient on their own.

Test plan items derived from the findings: (1) every interactive element measured at 320 px wide is at least 48x48 CSS px including expanded hit area and has at least 8 px gap; (2) rapid double/triple-tap on a tick, Done and Save does not double-fire or skip; (3) tap-and-slide-off cancels; (4) Undo toast works with TalkBack/VoiceOver and does not vanish while focused; (5) right and left layouts both reach every control with one thumb on a 6.7-inch-class screen (about 430 px wide); (6) reduced-motion on/off; (7) bottom controls not covered by the browser toolbar or gesture bar.
pitfalls: Do not treat 24 x 24 CSS px (WCAG 2.5.8 AA) as a design target; it is a legal floor. 44 px (2.5.5 AAA, Apple) and 48 px (Google, Lighthouse) are the practical thumb numbers, and the physical 9-10 mm result (Parhi 2006) is the most solid research basis.

Visual size is not hit size. Expanding hit areas with pseudo-elements or padding can cause neighbouring rows' hit areas to overlap; Lighthouse penalises overlap. Keep the 8 px gap or clip the expansion.

Mixed-up units: points (Apple), dp (Android) and CSS px are density-independent, but the 48 px = 9 mm equivalence only holds with a correct viewport meta tag; without width=device-width the browser may scale the layout.

'75 percent use their thumb' and '49 percent one-handed' are repeated with misattributions (some attribute 75 percent to Josh Clark, others to Hoober); the 49/36/15 grip split is better supported. Cite the grip split, not the 75 percent.

Hoober's 2013 observational data was gathered on 2013-era phones (smaller screens). Reach on 6.7-inch phones is worse for the top and far side; the app's bottom-right anchoring is consistent with this, but exact green/yellow/red maps are illustrative, not measured for your device sizes.

Fitts's law 'screen edge = infinitely large target' is a mouse-era argument; on touch, edge and corner targets are not easier. The bottom-right corner can also collide with the OS gesture area and rounded screen corners, so keep a margin and use safe-area insets.

Auto-dismissing undo toasts can fail assistive-technology users and users who need more time (WCAG 2.2.1); provide a persistent alternative such as a visible 'Undo last' control or extend/pause on focus.
Confirmation-dialog overuse trains users to tap through (dialog fatigue); a confirm button placed where the trigger button was is hit by a double-tap. Use sparingly and displace the confirm control.

Position:fixed and 100vh are unreliable in mobile browsers as the toolbar collapses; a never-scrolling fixed-viewport layout needs dvh/svh units and safe-area insets or the bottom-right controls will be hidden or jump.
Activating on pointerdown makes accidental taps unrecoverable and breaks scroll-to-cancel; make toggles fire on click/pointerup.
Color-only states (green done, amber skipped, grey pending) fail WCAG 1.4.1 and are a problem for colour-blind users; the Airplane and Modern skins both need the shape/text cue.

Gamification or celebratory animation after every tick may distract rather than help users with ADHD; evidence is contested. Keep completion feedback brief (under about 300 ms) and optional per checklist, as the app already does with sound/speech.

Long animations delay the next tap: if a tick animation or screen transition blocks input for over about 300-400 ms, fast users will double-tap and undo their own progress. Never block pointer input during feedback animation.
navigator.vibrate silently does nothing on iPhone; do not make haptics the only confirmation channel.

touch-action: manipulation removing the double-tap-zoom click delay is general knowledge not verified by these searches; modern mobile browsers largely eliminate the 300 ms delay when the viewport is width=device-width, which was also not verified here.

NN/g guidance on progress indicators for known-length task lists (x of y) and any direct research on checklist/step progress indicators improving completion was not found; the goal-gradient and endowed-progress evidence comes from loyalty-card field studies.

No peer-reviewed research specific to ADHD users and checklist/task apps was found; the ADHD design advice is practitioner opinion. Optimum tick-feedback timing for ADHD users specifically is unknown.

Whether Apple HIG text in full still reads '44x44 pt' on the current Buttons page was not confirmed by reading the page; confirmed only via forum quotes and the older UI Design Dos and Don'ts tips page.
Haptic and audio-latency numbers (target under 100 ms for tap-to-sound, 10-20 ms vibration pulse) are engineering suggestions from the 100 ms perception limit, not sourced findings.
cssTechniques: Hit-area tokens: :root { --hit-min: 48px; --hit-gap: 8px; --row-h: 56px; } and .row { min-block-size: var(--row-h); } so every skin inherits the same minimum while changing only visuals.

Expand hit area without changing look: .tick { position: relative; } .tick::before { content: ''; position: absolute; inset: -10px; } (clip so neighbouring expanded areas do not overlap; keep 8px gap).

Bottom-right anchored upward-growing stack: .stack { display: flex; flex-direction: column-reverse; justify-content: flex-start; align-items: flex-end; } so the first item sits at the bottom and the stack grows up.

Left-hand mirror: :root[data-hand='left'] .stack { align-items: flex-start; } and flip action rows with flex-direction: row-reverse, ideally using logical properties (inset-inline-end, margin-inline-start) with dir toggled on the app root.

Fixed viewport and safe areas: <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover'>; html, body { height: 100dvh; overflow: hidden; overscroll-behavior: none; } .dock { padding: 0 max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right)) max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)) 0; }
Scrollable exception only for the references page: .refs { overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain; -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch; }

Suppress accidental text selection / callout on rows and buttons: .row, button { user-select: none; -webkit-touch-callout: none; -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; touch-action: manipulation; }

Pressed feedback with asymmetric timing (instant in, short out): .row:active { transform: scale(.98); transition: none; } .row { transition: transform 120ms ease-out, background-color 160ms ease-out; }
Check-mark state change in 120-200ms using a CSS-only stroke-dashoffset or clip-path reveal; no JS animation loops.
Motion tokens: --t-press: 0ms; --t-tick: 160ms; --t-enter: 225ms; --t-exit: 195ms; --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1);

Reduced motion: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; animation-iteration-count: 1 !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; scroll-behavior: auto !important; } } and keep color/shape state changes intact.
Coarse-pointer sizing: @media (pointer: coarse) { :root { --row-h: 56px; } } and @media (hover: none) { .row:hover { background: none; } } so hover styles never stick after a tap.

Segmented progress bar with one segment per item: .progress { display: grid; grid-auto-flow: column; gap: 4px; } .progress > i { block-size: 8px; } .progress > i[data-done] { background: var(--accent); }, plus a text '3 / 8' for non-visual redundancy.

State shapes beyond color: pending = bordered empty box; done = check mark glyph (inline SVG or ::after); skipped = dash/slash glyph plus visible text label 'Skipped'; set aria-checked or aria-label text accordingly.
Focus visibility for switch/keyboard users: :focus-visible { outline: 3px solid var(--focus); outline-offset: 2px; } sized so the focus ring does not shrink the 48px hit area.

Undo toast placement: position: fixed; inset-inline-end: 16px; bottom: calc(var(--dock-h) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom) + 8px); above the primary action so it never covers the thumb's next target; keep the Undo button at least 48px high.

topic: Interface design that helps people with ADHD stay on task (cognitive load, one-thing-at-a-time focus, salience of the current step, motion, time-blindness aids, sound/haptics, reward vs gamification, dyslexia-friendly typography). Findings are labelled EVIDENCE (empirical study or meta-analysis), EXPERT GUIDANCE (standards bodies, heuristics, consensus) or FOLKLORE (plausible but untested, vendor or practitioner claims). Caveat: WebFetch could not reach w3.org, nngroup.com, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov or w3c.github.io (DNS failure), so everything below comes from WebSearch result summaries and not from reading the primary documents.

findings.claim: The W3C COGA Note is the main standards-body reference for cognitive accessibility. It is expert guidance, not experimental evidence.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE] 'Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities' is a W3C Working Group Note (April 2021). It is supplemental to WCAG, and following it is not required for WCAG conformance. It lists attention as a functional need, linked to ADD/ADHD, and its objectives include 'Help users focus' and 'Ensure processes do not rely on memory'. Each objective has patterns with use/avoid examples, user stories and test methods. A UK government summary lists eight objectives: understand what things are and how to use them; find what they need; clear content; avoid mistakes and correct them; help users focus; processes that do not rely on memory; help and support; adaptation and personalisation. I could not open the live document, so exact pattern names and wording are unconfirmed.

findings.claim: NN/g's usability heuristics support keeping state visible, using recognition over recall and keeping the UI minimal. These are expert heuristics, not ADHD-specific findings.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE] Visibility of system status: users should always know the current state and the outcome of their last action. Recognition rather than recall: interfaces should reduce memory load because short-term memory is limited. Aesthetic and minimalist design: every extra unit of information competes with the relevant ones and reduces their visibility. These map directly onto a run screen that shows the whole stack with ticks (state is visible, nothing has to be remembered).

findings.claim: Progressive disclosure ('show less at once') is widely recommended, but its empirical support is thin and over-application backfires.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE, weak empirical base] Secondary sources say the original authors (Carroll and Rosson) noted limited empirical evidence for its effectiveness, and that NN/g's recommendation is expert opinion. Known failure modes: hiding essential information, too many taps, and poor discoverability. I only saw this secondhand, not NN/g's own article.

findings.claim: No rigorous HCI study was found showing that one-thing-at-a-time screens reduce cognitive load in people with ADHD. The idea is plausible design folklore.
findings.detail: [FOLKLORE] Search found a student capstone project (UW 'Bearable') built around showing one task at a time, vendor blogs recommending 'one clear action', and an anecdote from an indie developer that a well-structured step list did not reduce load because the cost was anticipation, not information overload. A paper using NASA-TLX with children with ADHD on educational apps exists, but its results were not visible to me. For this app, whether to hide or dim not-yet-reached items is an open question that needs user testing.

findings.claim: Working-memory deficits in ADHD are well established in meta-analyses, which supports putting task state in the interface and not in the user's head.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE for the deficit; design implication is inference] Martinussen et al. (2005) meta-analysis of working-memory impairments in children with ADHD reported large effects for spatial storage (ES 0.85) and spatial central executive (ES 1.06). Kasper, Alderson and Hudec (2012, Clin Psychol Rev 32:605-617) found moderate overall effects across phonological and visuospatial modalities, with moderators explaining between-group differences. Almost all of this is child data and lab tasks. The step from 'working memory deficit' to 'show the checklist state on screen' is a reasonable design inference, not a tested UI result.

findings.claim: Smartphone notifications increase self-reported inattention and hyperactivity, even in people without ADHD.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, general population] Kushlev, Proulx and Dunn, CHI 2016: 221 UBC students spent one week with notification alerts on and phones within reach, and another week with alerts off and phones away, in a within-subject design. Inattention and hyperactivity scores were higher in the alerts-on week, and higher inattention predicted lower productivity and wellbeing. The sample was non-clinical and the outcome was self-report. This is an argument against push notifications and badges in an on-demand checklist app.

findings.claim: Enhanced distractibility is increasingly framed as a core feature of adult ADHD, but lab evidence on motion as a distractor is preliminary and inconsistent.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, weak] Panagiotidi, Overton and Stafford (Perception, 2017): non-clinical adults with more ADHD-like traits were less slowed by peripheral distractors shown 80 ms before targets, which is read as greater sensitivity to peripheral cues. A small preliminary fMRI poster (17 adults) found stronger superior-colliculus responses to moving than static distractors in higher-inattention participants, only for right-hemifield distractors. One thesis notes that classic lab measures have not consistently shown excess distractibility in ADHD. No study I found tests animated UI elements directly. Minimizing peripheral movement is sensible but is extrapolation.

findings.claim: Time-perception deficits in ADHD are real and replicated in meta-analyses.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE for the deficit] A meta-analysis of altered perceptual timing in ADHD found broad deficits in time estimation and production. Noreika, Falter and Rubia (2013, Neuropsychologia 51:235-266) reviewed neurocognitive and neuroimaging evidence and treat timing as a key deficit linked to impulsiveness and inattention. A 2020 J Attention Disorders meta-analysis (27 studies, children and adolescents) reported less accurate time perception (Hedges' g above 0.40), less precise perception (g = 0.66) and a tendency to overestimate time. A separate 55-study meta-analysis found worse discrimination of very brief durations, especially sub-second.

findings.claim: No controlled trial was found showing that visual timers or countdowns improve on-task behavior in ADHD. Support is practitioner and vendor material.
findings.detail: [FOLKLORE] Searches for visual-timer or time-elapsed interventions returned retail pages, app listings and blogs; one retailer page attributed benefits to Child Mind Institute studies that I could not verify. The mechanism ('make time visible, reduce mental effort of estimating time left') is plausible given the timing-deficit meta-analyses, but it is untested. A Stanford student need-finding report found adults with ADHD often struggle to estimate task duration, which is design research, not an efficacy trial.

findings.claim: Periodic alerting cues give a short-lived improvement in sustained attention in children with ADHD, not a block-wide one.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, small sample] A 2006 study of 15 children with ADHD and 15 matched controls used a modified SART with 8 random non-contingent alerts in two blocks. Alerts produced a significant short-term drop in commission errors right after each cue but did not reduce total commission errors over the block. Implication: sound or haptic cues help briefly, so they work best as discrete confirmations tied to an action and not as constant nagging.

findings.claim: No ADHD-specific efficacy evidence was found for haptic (vibration) reminders. Habituation is a documented concern.
findings.detail: [FOLKLORE / evidence gap] An NYU group notes that fixed or intermittent vibration cues for self-monitoring exist and reduce stigma but are vulnerable to habituation; their personalised-timing device had no outcome data in what I saw. Patents describe tactile reminders without efficacy data. A 45-adult study found no difference between low- and high-ADHD-symptom groups in distraction by vibration, but the high-symptom group missed more trials.

findings.claim: Background noise can help some children with ADHD (Moderate Brain Arousal model), but this concerns ambient noise, not discrete UI tick sounds.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, partly contested] Soderlund et al. (2007) found white noise improved memory performance in children with ADHD and worsened it in controls. A review cites a meta-analysis of 13 white-noise studies with small to medium effects, though I could not confirm which paper that is. One summary notes a 100 Hz tone gave the same benefit as pink noise, which challenges the stochastic-resonance explanation. Relevance to a short tick sound is weak, so do not use this to justify background audio.

findings.claim: ADHD research shows a strong preference for immediate over delayed rewards (delay aversion), which supports immediate, small feedback on each tick.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE in lab tasks; UI application is inference] Marco et al. (2009, 360 ADHD probands) found children with ADHD chose smaller-sooner rewards more often than controls, and more so when the sooner option also shortened the wait. Yu and Sonuga-Barke (2020) found steeper discounting in ADHD only when children actually had to wait, not when they imagined waiting. Children with ADHD also prefer reward immediacy over high reward rate or task ease. Design implication: confirm each tick instantly (under about 100 ms) and avoid making feedback wait on animations or a final summary.

findings.claim: Evidence that gamification helps people with ADHD is small and mixed. Reviews flag lack of controls and a risk that game elements distract.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, weak] A scoping review of 19 mobile-game studies found performance improved while playing, but evidence of effectiveness is scarce and mixed, with small samples, no control groups and narrow outcomes. A PRISMA review of 13 neurofeedback-gamification studies noted a systematic lack of well-powered controlled studies and the risk that game elements add distraction. A meta-analysis of 27 RCTs of gamified digital mental-health interventions reported a small effect for ADHD (Hedges' g = 0.28). A newer 24-RCT meta-analysis on gamification for children and adolescents with ADHD exists, but I saw only its announcement. I could not map each statistic to a specific URL with certainty.

findings.claim: Extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation (overjustification), but the effect is context-dependent and its applicability to points, badges and streaks is contested.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, contested] Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, Psychological Bulletin 125:627-668) meta-analysed 128 experiments and found expected tangible rewards contingent on performance reduce intrinsic motivation, while verbal praise did not. The effect needs pre-existing intrinsic motivation, and later commentary doubts whether points and badges count as the rewards studied. Self-determination theory reviews conclude gamification can both support and undermine motivation depending on whether it supports autonomy and competence. The specific effect sizes (about d = -0.40 and +0.31) came from a consultant's blog and are not verified.

findings.claim: The claim that streaks harm users after a break (anxiety, abandonment) rests on vendor blogs. No peer-reviewed evidence was found, although the loss-aversion mechanism is plausible.
findings.detail: [FOLKLORE] Vendor and blog sources assert that broken streaks suppress later engagement and cite a 2023 Journal of Consumer Research paper (Silverman and Barasch) that I could not verify. Retention claims (for example a 20-40% DAU lift) are unsourced marketing. A checklist-prompt app is not a habit tracker, so it has no natural need for streaks.

findings.claim: Most ADHD technology research frames ADHD as a deficit to correct, with little co-design, and participants push back on that framing.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, critical literature review] Spiel, Hornecker, Williams and Good (CHI 2022, DOI 10.1145/3491102.3517592) reviewed ADHD technologies in Computing/HCI: most aim to reduce traits that conflict with neurotypical norms, few involve people with ADHD in setting goals or designing, and participants resisted deficit framing. Implication: give users control (opt-in aids, adjustable settings) and use neutral, non-shaming copy.

findings.claim: If-then planning (implementation intentions) improved response inhibition in children with ADHD in lab tasks.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, small lab studies in children] Gawrilow and Gollwitzer (2008, Cognitive Therapy and Research 32:261-280): in Study 1, children with ADHD who paired a goal with an if-then plan reached the Go/No-Go inhibition level of children without ADHD. In Study 2, combining if-then plans with stimulant medication gave the best result. A related 2011 paper reported better delay of gratification after if-then plans. Possible design link: an optional 'when' trigger line on a checklist. This is a feature idea, not a validated UI pattern.

findings.claim: Checklists have strong but contested evidence in medicine. Implementation quality matters.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, not ADHD-specific] Haynes et al. (WHO, NEJM 2009): 7,688 surgical patients in 8 countries, 19-item checklist, complications fell by more than a third. A later NEJM crisis-checklist study reported a 74% lower chance of missing a critical process of care. Critics note that Pronovost's ICU programme bundled many interventions, and that the Ontario mandate gave disappointing results. A BMJ head-to-head (Urbach and Dimick vs Haynes and Gawande) shows the debate is unresolved. Lesson: a checklist works when it is actually used at the point of action, so friction in the run screen matters more than features.

findings.claim: Salient visual cues improve resumption after interruption and can prevent skipped final steps. This is general human-factors evidence, not ADHD-specific.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, general population, partly secondhand] Altmann and Trafton's goal-activation model says suspended goals decay and cues in the environment can re-activate them. Trafton, Altmann and Brock (2005) reportedly found a highly salient cue speeded resumption. Chung and Byrne (2008) reportedly found a prominent hint just before the post-completion step eliminated post-completion errors (the habit of skipping the last step). Ratwani and colleagues found that keeping a spatial representation of the primary task helps resumption, which argues for stable item positions. Highlighting the current step specifically is less directly tested.

findings.claim: WCAG 2.2.2 (Level A) requires a pause/stop/hide mechanism for auto-starting motion longer than 5 seconds. 2.3.3 (AAA) requires interaction-triggered motion to be disableable. prefers-reduced-motion is the main mechanism.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE / standard] 2.2.2 covers moving, blinking, scrolling and auto-updating content; the understanding page widens 'starts automatically' to include content started by focus, hover or scrolling into view. Pausing only while focused does not count. 2.3.3 covers animation triggered by user action unless essential; honouring prefers-reduced-motion is the primary implementation. Reduced motion must not hide content. Flashing is handled separately under Guideline 2.3.

findings.claim: web.dev recommends a no-motion-first default and replacing spatial motion (slide, zoom, parallax) with opacity fades.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE] web.dev's motion lesson says you cannot predict what movement triggers seizure, vestibular or other issues, so its example defaults to no animation and opts users in with prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference. Secondary guides add that opacity fades are generally safe for motion-sensitive users, and that parallax, zoom and spinning elements are the most common violations.

findings.claim: WCAG 2.5.8 sets a minimum pointer target of 24x24 CSS px (AA). This is a floor, not a comfort target for one-handed thumb use.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE] New in WCAG 2.2: targets at least 24x24 CSS px, or undersized targets with enough spacing, measured on the hit area and not the visible graphic. Exceptions include inline text links, user-agent controlled targets and equivalent controls. Sources I saw were third-party summaries of the W3C text.

findings.claim: Extra-large letter spacing improved reading accuracy and speed in children with dyslexia (Zorzi et al. 2012). This is the best-supported typographic lever found.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, with limits] PNAS 109(28):11455-11459. About 74 Italian and French children with dyslexia read short sentences in 14 pt Times New Roman with default spacing vs +2.5 pt letter spacing (word and line spacing widened proportionally). Accuracy roughly doubled and speed rose by more than 20%. Children without dyslexia showed no benefit, and letter spacing was the critical factor. The authors link it to crowding and call it a supplement to training. Skottun and Skoyles questioned specificity to dyslexia; Zorzi et al. replied. Limits: short sentences, children, print or screen of one font, so transfer to long phone text is inference.

findings.claim: Specialised 'dyslexia fonts' (OpenDyslexic) showed no reading benefit. Plain sans-serif or monospaced fonts did as well or better.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE] Wery and Diliberto (Annals of Dyslexia 2017): single-subject alternating-treatment design with elementary students with dyslexia, comparing OpenDyslexic with Arial and Times New Roman on letter naming, word reading and nonword reading. No gain in rate or accuracy, and no student preferred OpenDyslexic. Rello and Baeza-Yates (ASSETS 2013, DOI 10.1145/2513383.2513447): eye-tracking, 48 participants with dyslexia, 12 fonts. Sans-serif and monospaced fonts (Helvetica, Courier, Arial, Verdana, CMU; lists differ slightly between sources) did best, italic did worst, OpenDyslexic was not easier to read. Small samples.

findings.claim: British Dyslexia Association style guidance recommends sans-serif type at roughly 12-14 pt, line spacing around 1.5, left-aligned text, and avoiding all-caps, italics and underline. It is expert consensus and partly ahead of the evidence.
findings.detail: [EXPERT GUIDANCE] Figures vary by summary (12-14 pt, or 12-15 pt; some suggest letter and word spacing up by 30-35% of font size). One review notes recent evidence shows no consistent sans-serif advantage over serif and no consistent advantage for specialised dyslexia fonts. I read secondary summaries, not the BDA guide itself.

findings.claim: Bionic Reading (bolded word starts) has no demonstrated benefit. The only large test is from a vendor with a competing product.
findings.detail: [FOLKLORE] Readwise timed about 2,000 readers and found no speed benefit (average 2.6 wpm slower). A small 2025 study of 60 Iranian EFL learners reported gains in adults without ADHD or dyslexia. I found no ADHD or dyslexia trials, and a Utrecht EEG thesis on ADHD was only visible as a description.

findings.claim: ADHD and reading disorders co-occur at high rates, so the reading-heavy references page should be designed for both.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE] Estimates of learning disorder among children with ADHD range from 20% to 60%. In the German GINIplus/LISAplus cohorts (Czamara et al. 2013, PLoS ONE), children with ADHD symptoms had about 2.8 times the odds of reading or spelling difficulties. Reviews point to shared genetic and neuropsychological mechanisms, and to inattention more than hyperactivity as the link. Prevalence figures vary a lot by sample and diagnostic criteria; I found no true pooled meta-analysis.

findings.claim: Existing ADHD apps are mostly self-tests, information tools, task aids and brain-training games, with little rigorous evaluation of task-support UI.
findings.detail: [EVIDENCE, landscape] A JMIR mHealth 2016 review of Google Play and iTunes found most apps were self-testing and information tools, task and scheduling aids, and brain-training games, mostly targeting patients directly. A 2018 feasibility study of an ADHD app prototype with 6 adults rated it moderately to very helpful, but the sample is tiny. This confirms the evidence base for UI patterns in this space is thin.

recommendations: Treat the Classic design as the calm baseline and make all three designs share identical behaviour, layout and stack order. Designs may change only colour, type, borders, shadows and texture. The best evidence (WCAG, COGA, delay aversion, resumption cues) concerns behaviour and feedback, not skin. [Basis: expert guidance + inference]

Keep the whole stack visible and make the next unticked item the single most salient element through size, border weight, contrast or a position marker, not through animation. Dim or soften ticked items but keep them legible, and never reorder or move items when ticked, because stable spatial positions aid resumption. Whether to hide future items is untested; if offered at all, make it a user setting, not a default. [Basis: resumption-cue evidence + NN/g recognition-over-recall; one-at-a-time benefit is folklore]

Give instant, single, quiet confirmation on each tick: state change in under about 100 ms, plus the existing optional short tick sound and spoken confirmation. Always pair audio or haptic with a visual change so no single modality is required, and do not queue feedback behind animation. [Basis: delay-aversion lab evidence + small alerting study; application is inference]

Do not use points, levels, streaks, leaderboards, confetti or looping celebration. If any reward exists, make it one brief, factual completion state ('Done, 7 of 7') that is optional to dismiss. Gamification evidence in ADHD is small and mixed, streak harm is unverified, and overjustification is plausible for extrinsic rewards. This is a checklist prompt app, not a habit tracker. [Basis: mixed evidence + restraint]

Show progress as text plus a static bar ('3 of 7'), updated on tick only. Offer time-blindness aids as opt-in, per checklist: an optional expected-duration line per item or checklist, and an optional count-up elapsed time updated at coarse intervals (for example every minute) in plain text. Avoid ticking second-by-second countdowns, red urgency states and auto-advance. Efficacy of visual timers is untested, so ship them as optional and observe. [Basis: timing-deficit meta-analyses (evidence) + untested timer folklore]

Make the Done/Close step hard to skip but easy to undo: show a clear 'N items left' state near the Done button, and flag required items without blocking silently. Provide undo for accidental ticks (misses happen one-handed). The post-completion-error literature suggests the final step is the most likely to be dropped. [Basis: post-completion-error evidence, partly secondhand]
Send no push notifications, badges or reminders. Runs are user-initiated, so keep it that way. [Basis: Kushlev et al., CHI 2016]

Motion policy: no-motion-first. Put every transition inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference), keep them at or under about 150 ms, use opacity or colour changes instead of slides, zooms or parallax, and never loop or autoplay. Neobrutalist press effects (shadow shift) and airplane-style needle sweeps must degrade to instant state changes. Add an in-app 'Reduce effects' setting that applies to all three designs (flat shadows, no grain, no transitions), because the OS preference is not always set. [Basis: WCAG 2.2.2/2.3.3, web.dev]

Typography: use a plain sans-serif (or a monospaced face for the airplane look) at 16 px or larger for body text; no 'dyslexia font'. For the long references page use line-height about 1.5, left-aligned text (no justify), short paragraphs with real headings, and slightly increased letter-spacing and word-spacing (letter-spacing about 0.05 to 0.12em). Avoid italics, all-caps for running text, and underline for emphasis. Consider a Settings control for text spacing. [Basis: Zorzi 2012, Rello 2013, BDA guidance; exact values are inference]

Keep text on solid, high-contrast surfaces in all designs. In the Modern design, use gradients and grain only on backgrounds and large decorative areas, not under body text or tick boxes. In the Airplane design, never encode state by colour alone (amber/green must be paired with a glyph or word). Keep strong, flat tick-box borders. [Basis: WCAG contrast principles, COGA 'help users focus'; grain/gradient effects on ADHD or dyslexia readers are untested]

Use big, whole-row tap targets well above the WCAG 24 px floor (roughly 56 px row height), with spacing between rows, anchored to the bottom-right for the right thumb. Add touch-action: manipulation to avoid double-tap delay and accidental zoom. [Basis: WCAG 2.5.8 floor; ergonomic figures are from prior knowledge, not retrieved]

Use neutral, non-judgemental copy ('2 items left', not 'You missed 2'). Give users control over every aid (sound, spoken confirmation, timers, spacing, reduce effects) and avoid deficit framing. [Basis: Spiel et al., CHI 2022]

Consider an optional single-line 'when' trigger per checklist (for example 'When I leave the house'), displayed on the Ask or Run header, as a lightweight implementation intention. Label it as an experiment. [Basis: Gawrilow and Gollwitzer 2008, children, lab; feature idea only]

Because evidence for task-support UI in adults with ADHD is thin, validate with real neurodivergent users. Measure skipped items, time to first tick, abandoned runs and subjective load (NASA-TLX was used in the one child-ADHD app study found). Test the three designs against each other on these measures. [Basis: Spiel et al. critique + evidence gaps]
pitfalls: Presenting design folklore as science. Claims that visual timers, one-task-at-a-time screens, streaks or 'dopamine-friendly' gamification help ADHD users are mostly from vendor blogs, practitioner posts and student projects. Only timing deficits, working-memory deficits, delay aversion and letter-spacing effects have actual studies behind them, and most are child or lab data.

Gamification overreach: points, badges, streaks and confetti compete for attention, can feel controlling (overjustification), and reviews warn of distraction. Streak-break harm is unverified but plausible, and a checklist app has no need for streaks.

Urgency timers: ticking countdowns, red flashing or auto-advancing steps raise time pressure and break WCAG 2.2.1-style time-limit expectations (COGA also asks for adjustable timing). No evidence says countdowns help; the timing literature supports making time visible, not making it stressful.

Decorative motion and celebration animation: motion can pull attention in peripheral vision, vestibular users can be harmed, and WCAG 2.2.2/2.3.3 apply. Do not rely on prefers-reduced-motion alone; also provide an in-app switch.

Dyslexia-font and Bionic-Reading marketing: OpenDyslexic showed no benefit, and Bionic Reading has no credible evidence. Do not ship or advertise them as accessibility features. Spacing, plain sans-serif type and left alignment are better supported.

Over-applied progressive disclosure: hiding items or details can remove the overview, increase anticipation anxiety (anecdotal) and hurt discoverability. The stack is the point of this product; test before hiding anything.

Single-modality feedback: sound-only or haptic-only confirmation fails when the phone is muted or the device does not support it (Vibration API support on iOS Safari is from prior knowledge, not retrieved). Haptics also habituate. Always show a visual state change too.

Colour-only state in the Airplane design (amber/green/cyan) and low-contrast text over gradients or grain in the Modern design. These can hurt both dyslexic and ADHD readers. Coloured-overlay and 'visual stress' claims are contested and were not verified here.

Extrapolating from children, lab tasks and small samples to adults using a phone one-handed. Most ADHD effect sizes here come from children (Martinussen, Marco, Gawrilow), and several UI claims come from general-population studies (Kushlev, Trafton).

Deficit-framed language and surprise behaviour: copy that scolds, auto-completing or auto-skipping items, and hidden settings. Spiel et al. found participants resist deficit framing, and COGA stresses predictability and user control.

Mis-taps from one-handed use: items too small or too close together, accidental double-taps firing sound twice, or no undo. These are interaction bugs that matter more than visual style, and worth explicit test scenarios (rapid taps, tap-then-undo, tapping while audio is playing, interrupted runs, rotated or resized viewport).
cssTechniques: Current-step salience without motion: mark the next item with a thicker border or outline (outline: 3px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px), larger size or weight, and a leading marker glyph. Ticked items use a muted colour token that still meets 4.5:1 text contrast; do not rely on opacity below about 0.6 for text.

No-motion-first transitions: write base styles with no transitions, then add transition: background-color .12s, border-color .12s, transform .12s only inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference). Provide a [data-reduce-effects] root attribute that sets *, *::before, *::after { transition: none !important; animation: none !important } for the in-app Reduce effects setting.

Stable layout: reserve fixed row heights (min-height: 56px or more) and use contain: layout on rows so ticking never shifts neighbours. Use flex-direction: column-reverse (or order) on the stack so the first item sits at the bottom and the list grows upward.

Instant tick feedback: change checked state on pointerdown or click using :active and [aria-checked=true] styles, so feedback lands within one frame. Use touch-action: manipulation; -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; user-select: none on rows.

Progress without animation: a <progress> element or a div with transform: scaleX(var(--done)) set once per tick (no transition when reduced motion is requested), paired with a text label such as '3 of 7'.

Elapsed time as text: update a plain-text 'elapsed' element at coarse intervals (for example per minute) instead of a continuously animated ring. Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums so digits do not jitter.

Reading typography for the references page: font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.4vw, 1.125rem); line-height: 1.5; letter-spacing: 0.05em to 0.12em; word-spacing: 0.1em to 0.16em; text-align: left; hyphens: manual; max-width about 60ch; margin-block between paragraphs about 1em or more; font-style normal for emphasis (use font-weight instead of italics); no text-decoration underline for emphasis.
Headings and wrap: text-wrap: balance for short titles and text-wrap: pretty for body text, so lines end cleanly. Avoid text-transform: uppercase on running text (labels only, with letter-spacing).

Neobrutalism and grain safely: hard offset shadows (box-shadow: 4px 4px 0 var(--ink)) and thick borders are static and fine. Press feedback via transform: translate(2px,2px) only under no-preference motion. Put feTurbulence grain on a body::before layer with pointer-events: none and low opacity, and drop it from text containers (the references page) and when [data-reduce-effects] is set.

Gradients behind content: apply gradients to the page background and decorative blocks only; put body text and tick boxes on solid surface colour tokens. Redefine tokens for dark/light per design rather than inverting automatically.

Targets and ergonomics: whole row as the hit area, padding-inline and padding-block for at least 56 px height, gap of at least 8 px between rows, and a larger tick box (around 40 px) on the right edge. Keep primary actions in the bottom-right quadrant with padding: env(safe-area-inset-bottom).
Fixed viewport without scroll: height: 100dvh; overflow: hidden on the app shell, with overflow: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain only on the references page's inner list.

Font choice from Google Fonts: a plain sans-serif for Classic and Modern, a monospaced or plain grotesque for Airplane. Do not add a 'dyslexia font'. Atkinson Hyperlegible and Lexend are available on Google Fonts, but I did not verify any ADHD or dyslexia benefit for either (see unverified).
unverified: I could not open any primary page: WebFetch failed with DNS errors for www.w3.org, w3c.github.io, www.nngroup.com and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov. All findings come from WebSearch result summaries, so the exact wording and numbering of COGA objectives and patterns, and NN/g's own text on progressive disclosure, are unconfirmed.

The 'Help users focus' and 'Ensure processes do not rely on memory' objective names come from a UK government summary and search snippets of the W3C Note. I did not see the specific patterns (for example on distraction, time limits or progress), so their names and wording could not be quoted.

Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999) effect sizes (d = -0.40 for expected tangible rewards, +0.31 for verbal praise, 128 experiments) came from a gamification consultant's blog and were not checked against the paper.

The Silverman and Barasch (2023, Journal of Consumer Research) paper on broken streaks, cited by a gamification blog, was not found. The loss-aversion ratio of about 2 to 2.5 times also had no primary source.

Which specific URL carries the Hedges' g = 0.28 gamified-intervention meta-analysis (27 RCTs) versus the 19-study mobile-game scoping review versus the 13-study neurofeedback-gamification review; I cited one Frontiers link for the group and the mapping may be off. The newer 24-RCT ADHD gamification meta-analysis was seen only as an event announcement.
The 'Pickens 2023' white-noise meta-analysis could not be found. A review cites a 13-study meta-analysis with small-to-medium effects, but I could not confirm its authors.
Kofler 2013 and any Rohde/Schwartz timing paper (named in one of my queries) were not found or confirmed, and I make no claim from them.
The results of the UNISON study of children with ADHD using NASA-TLX across input devices were not visible, so I cannot say whether touchscreens raised or lowered cognitive load.

The Zorzi 2012 sample of 74 children comes from news coverage of the paper; one search summary only showed F(1,70). Whether the benefit holds for adult readers, phone screens or other fonts was not established. Skottun and Skoyles' criticism and Zorzi's reply were seen only as titles.

The results of the 2016 PubMed study on letter spacing and coloured overlays in adult dyslexia, and of Galliussi et al. 2020 (inter-letter spacing and inter-word spacing), were not visible. The Meares-Irlen 'visual stress' and coloured-overlay claims were not researched.
Whether Lexend or Atkinson Hyperlegible have any peer-reviewed evidence for ADHD or dyslexia readers was not searched.

CSS and ergonomic figures not retrieved this session (from prior knowledge): WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing values (letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, line-height 1.5, paragraph spacing 2em); the 1.4.3 contrast ratio of 4.5:1 and 1.4.11 non-text contrast of 3:1; platform tap-target guidance of about 44-48 px; and Vibration API support gaps on iOS Safari. Verify before relying on them.

WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable was not found in search results, so the statement that countdowns and auto-advance conflict with it rests on prior knowledge and COGA's general emphasis on adjustable timing.

No peer-reviewed study was found on: visual timers or elapsed-time displays improving on-task behaviour in ADHD; haptic reminders in ADHD; animated UI elements as distractors in ADHD; one-thing-at-a-time interfaces reducing cognitive load in ADHD; streak mechanics in ADHD. These remain design hypotheses.
Interruption-resumption claims (Trafton, Altmann and Brock 2005; Chung and Byrne 2008) were seen only as secondary summaries of the papers and are not ADHD-specific.
The 2006 periodic-alerts SART study (15 children with ADHD, 15 controls) was seen only as a DeepDyve abstract; I did not confirm its authors or journal, and it is a small sample.

topic: Airliner cockpit display conventions (Boeing EICAS/PFD/ND/ECL and Airbus ECAM/PFD): color semantics, typography (B612 and Google Fonts alternatives), dark backgrounds, boxes/bezels, and how checklist lines and completed items are drawn. Method note: WebFetch was blocked in this sandbox (DNS failure and a proxy 403 on fonts.google.com, lii.enac.fr, patents.google.com and easa.europa.eu), so every finding comes from WebSearch result summaries. No primary page was read in full. No source found states exact hex values for any cockpit color.

findings.claim: Regulatory baseline: warning is red, caution is amber or yellow, and advisory alerts must not be red or green. Red, amber and yellow elsewhere on the flight deck must be limited.
findings.detail: 14 CFR 25.1322 (effective 2011, Amdt 25-131) is summarized as: red for warning, amber or yellow for caution, any color except red or green for advisory alerts. Red/amber/yellow for non-alerting functions must be limited so they do not harm crew alerting. The 2010 FAA NPRM wording excluded red, amber, yellow and green for advisories, so the final-rule wording is medium confidence. EASA CS-25.1322 carries the same limited-use rule. EASA's comment response says it would not distinguish yellow from amber, and records Airbus wanting existing yellow and green usage kept for commonality.

findings.claim: Airbus ECAM color meanings: red = warning (most urgent), amber = caution, green = normal, white = titles/labels/remarks, blue (cyan) = actions to be carried out or limitations, magenta = special/particular messages.
findings.detail: Airbus's own EASA comment states it complies with red for warnings and amber for cautions, and that green indicates normal while an alert generally represents something non-normal. The fuller legend comes from secondary sources and is consistent across them. Red means stop other tasks, amber means finish the current task then handle it. Blue/cyan is an action or selection still to be done (for example the procedure steps). Magenta marks special messages such as T.O. INHIBIT and LDG INHIBIT on the E/WD. White also marks a controlled function set to a non-normal position (for example a switch moved to OFF). The FlyByWire A32NX docs match this on the STS page: blue for limitations and procedures, white for approach procedures and cancelled cautions, amber for inoperative systems, green for information.

findings.claim: On the Airbus E/WD, normal system values are green and amber X marks mean information is unavailable. Amber pulsing on a parameter is an early warning of an approaching limit.
findings.detail: FlyByWire's ECAM pages (a simulation of the real system) show green for normal-range indications such as hydraulic pressure and amber 'X' for data not available. A secondary guide describes pulsing amber on SD-page parameters as a pre-warning.

findings.claim: Boeing EICAS uses three alert levels (A warning, B caution, C advisory) and a six-color palette: red, yellow/amber, cyan, magenta, white, green.
findings.detail: A 757 EICAS training slide lists the multicolor presentation as red, yellow, cyan (light blue), magenta (pink), white and green. A general EICAS reference associates red with warnings, yellow with caution/advisory messages, cyan with parameter names and status marks, and magenta with in-flight engine starting. These sources are generic or from the 757, not 777 or 787, so the mapping for newer types is not confirmed. They also state that colors and message categories vary by type.

findings.claim: Boeing electronic checklist (ECL) convention: incomplete items are white and completed items turn green. Operational notes are shown in blue so they stand apart from both.
findings.detail: Boeing's electronic checklist patent US 5454074 describes completed items (open-loop and closed-loop) changing text color from white to green, with notes displayed in blue. A related patent, US 5522026, describes the same white-pending / green-complete scheme. An MIT 16.422 lecture summary (secondary) also says incomplete items are white and complete items green. These are 1990s patent descriptions, so they may not match current 787 pixels.

findings.claim: Boeing ECL sensed vs non-sensed items: sensed (closed-loop) items turn green only when the aircraft confirms the state. Open-loop items need a manual cursor selection. A box marks the current item and jumps to the next incomplete one.
findings.detail: A Boeing paper (Boorman, 2001) says sensed line items will not turn green when the wrong switch is selected, and 'CHECKLIST COMPLETE' does not display until all items are complete. It also notes the current line-item box jumps to the next incomplete item when items are skipped. The 787 article in AIN says the ECL senses control positions and shows the item green if they agree, and unsensed items must be selected with the cursor. Patent text separates closed-loop (no crew response needed) from open-loop (crew response required) items.

findings.claim: Boeing ECL status model: a checklist can be completed, selected but not complete, not yet selected, overridden, or inhibited. On the 777 a checklist icon sits beside the EICAS message until the checklist is done.
findings.detail: MIT 16.422 lecture notes describe the 777 'checklist icon' beside an EICAS message whenever an ECL checklist still needs completing, removed once complete. A Boeing-assigned patent (surfaced in the same search; the exact patent number was not shown in the snippet) lists the same status states, including 'overridden'. MIT's summary also says the crew can deliberately override an item (example: inoperative autobrake) so the checklist can still be completed. How an overridden item is drawn (color or box style) was not found.

findings.claim: Airbus ECAM checklist/procedure interaction uses a blue selection box, not a filled highlight. The C/L key validates or devalidates the boxed item.
findings.detail: FlyByWire A380X docs (modelling the real A380 control panel): the up/down arrows move a blue box on the EWD. The box cannot surround a grey line except on the checklist menu. Pressing C/L validates or devalidates the boxed item, which is how items the ECAM cannot sense are ticked manually. Treat this as indicative for the A320 family rather than exact.

findings.claim: Airbus ECAM action lines: blue = still to do. Whether completed lines recolor, tick or are simply cleared was not confirmed.
findings.detail: Multiple secondary sources agree blue marks actions still to be carried out. One search summary reported completed actions being cleared (CLR key) rather than recolored, and found no per-line green tick on the A320. This conflicts with a common belief that Airbus shows a tick or green line for done items, which could not be verified. A green down-arrow on the ECAM indicates more steps below the visible screen (low confidence, source unnamed in the summary).

findings.claim: Airbus PFD flight mode annunciator (FMA) colors: green = engaged, blue/cyan = armed, magenta = altitude constraints, white = approach capabilities/status, amber = caution, red = significant degradation.
findings.detail: Taken from two Brainscape flashcard sets, so low reliability. SKYbrary gives the generic rule that active is usually green and armed white or blue, and that abbreviations vary by manufacturer. A claimed 'magenta = managed' rule was not supported by these sources. A mode-change highlight box with a 10 second timeout also could not be verified.

findings.claim: Boeing PFD/ND colors per a third-party explainer: magenta = selected targets, flight director and active FMC route. Green = active modes and engaged systems. White = scales, labels and armed modes. Cyan = background map info and selectable symbols. Amber = caution, red = warning.
findings.detail: This is a 737-focused simulator explainer, not Boeing documentation. It notes the presentation differs between 737 Classic, NG and MAX and that no universal standard exists. No 777 or 787 specifics were found. It also warns that magenta guidance alone does not prove a mode is engaged.

findings.claim: B612 and B612 Mono: an open-source typeface family designed for aircraft cockpit screens. Airbus started the research in 2010 with ENAC and Universite de Toulouse. It was designed by Intactile DESIGN with ENAC, and is on Google Fonts.
findings.detail: ENAC page and PolarSys repository: collaboration began in 2010 (project members Laurent Spaggiari of Airbus, Jean-Luc Vinot of ENAC, Sylvie Athenes of Universite de Toulouse III, Yves Rinato of Intactile DESIGN). Design credited to Nicolas Chauveau, Thomas Paillot and Jonathan Favre-Lamarine (Intactile) with Jean-Luc Vinot, around 2012. Airbus agreed to release it under the Eclipse Public License via PolarSys in 2017. It won an Observeur du Design award (Industry Star) in 2018. The family is roman and italic in two weights (regular, bold) plus B612 Mono, and the name refers to the Little Prince's asteroid. Google Fonts describes it as 'designed and tested to be used on aircraft cockpit screens'. The ENAC page describes it as for future Airbus programs, so use in current production cockpits is not confirmed.

findings.claim: B612 design rules: maximize distance between letterforms to avoid confusion, keep open counterforms, keep each letter's distinguishing features, and use light traps at stroke junctions. It avoids monoline strokes with no thickness contrast.
findings.detail: PolarSys lists its main characteristics as maximizing the distance between character forms, respecting letter primitives, and harmonizing forms and spacing. ENAC says the designers excluded linear marks with no thickness contrast, as used in the CDS font of actual cockpits, and kept bowls open. Light traps are explained as helping in poor viewing conditions (lighting, viewing angle, high cognitive load). Secondary sources add that 0/O and 1/I/l are deliberately differentiated. Some commenters find the light traps distracting at large sizes and the narrow letter gap less readable (Hacker News).

findings.claim: Overpass Mono is the monospaced sibling of Overpass, itself an interpretation of Highway Gothic (US FHWA traffic-sign alphabets). It was designed by Delve Withrington (Delve Fonts) and sponsored by Red Hat and Google Fonts.
findings.detail: Google Fonts says Overpass interprets the Highway Gothic letterforms from the FHWA Standard Alphabets for Traffic Control Devices, with adjustments for on-screen legibility. Sources conflict on how many weights Overpass Mono has (four per Typewolf, five from Light to Bold per RightFont), so check the current Google Fonts page. It is licensed under the OFL. It is a sign-lettering grotesque, not a cockpit font, but its signage heritage gives a related instrument-panel feel.

findings.claim: Barlow, by Jeremy Tribby, is a slightly rounded, low-contrast grotesk inspired by California public signage (plates, highway signs, buses, trains). It comes in Normal, Semi Condensed and Condensed widths, each with 9 weights and italics.
findings.detail: The Google Fonts description matches. The three widths make Semi Condensed and Condensed useful for fitting long labels at 320px. Licensed under the OFL. The California-signage inspiration is stylistic, with no documented tie to an official sign standard. Barlow is not an aviation font. It suits a cockpit-like label look (similar to ARINC-era caps labels) only by resemblance.

findings.claim: Share Tech Mono (Carrois Apostrophe) ships in a single weight (400), OFL licensed, with a proportional companion Share Tech. IBM Plex Mono (Mike Abbink with Bold Monday) is OFL-licensed, with true italics and multiple weights.
findings.detail: Fontsource and Google Fonts listings show Share Tech Mono at weight 400 only, so there is no bold; bold would be synthesized. IBM Plex Mono: Wikipedia says the Plex family has eight weights with true italics, released under SIL OFL 1.1. The exact weight set served by Google Fonts for Plex Mono was not confirmed. Neither font was designed for cockpits. Share Tech Mono has a technical, squared, instrument-like look and Plex Mono is more neutral and humanist.

findings.claim: Airbus 'dark cockpit' / 'lights out' philosophy: pushbutton lights stay off when a system is normal. A lit light means a fault or a non-normal switch state ('white means you did it' is a common rule of thumb).
findings.detail: Airbus presentation material and Flightradar24's Boeing/Airbus explainer describe this. The term 'dark, quiet cockpit' is tied to Airbus-era design (A300, 1982 per FlightGlobal, details paywalled). A 'Boeing quiet and dark' doctrine could not be confirmed from an authoritative source. The takeaway for display design is minimal chrome in the normal state, with color reserved for state changes.

findings.claim: Cockpit display backgrounds are black, and dimmability is required for dark adaptation. The FAA recommends six or fewer colors across the flight deck.
findings.detail: FAA guidance says electronic displays should be dimmable to levels that allow dark adaptation while keeping outside vision and an acceptable presentation. The FAA reportedly recommends using six or fewer colors in a typical flight deck (low confidence; from FAA committee minutes summarized via search). A DTIC report says NVG-compatible cockpit lighting is typically green with no red. No source in this run explained why backgrounds are black beyond light-on-dark being the norm for dim environments.

findings.claim: The formal color standards are paywalled: SAE ARP4032B (color on electronic aircraft displays) and ARP4102/7 (display symbology). No chromaticity or RGB values are publicly stated in anything found.
findings.detail: NASA Ames's Color Usage site (colorusage.arc.nasa.gov) has pages on color usage hierarchy, background colors and aerospace graphics, but their contents were not retrieved. ARINC 661 explicitly does not specify look and feel. SAE ARP5289A also says it gives no specific recommendations on color or fonts. Hence any hex value for 'cockpit green' or 'cockpit amber' is an approximation.

cssTechniques: Color tokens as custom properties with semantic names, not hue names: --ok (green), --pending (white), --action (cyan), --caution (amber), --warn (red), --special (magenta), --bg (near-black). Redefine per theme; a cockpit look is dark-only, so supply a dimmed 'night' variant by lowering saturation or lightness rather than inventing a light theme.

Approximate palette on black (design suggestions, NOT from any source): green about #00FF66 to #3DF07A, white about #F2F2F2, cyan about #00E5FF to #00FFFF, amber about #FFB000 to #FFC000, red about #FF3030, magenta about #FF40FF, background about #000000 to #06080B. Use these as starting points only. Avoid pure blue (#0000FF), whose contrast on black is only about 2.4:1 (my calculation, not from a source), which is the practical reason cockpits use cyan for 'blue'.

Checklist line anatomy copied from Boeing ECL: pending line = white text with an empty square box on the right; done line = green text with a green check in the box; note/detail line = cyan or blue text, indented, smaller; required-and-unchecked at Done = amber text and amber box outline.

Current-item indicator as a thin cyan outline box around the line (border: 2px solid var(--action); no fill), matching the Airbus blue selection box and the Boeing current-line-item box. Keep it a box rather than a filled highlight so text contrast is unchanged.

Label typography: uppercase, letter-spacing about 0.04em to 0.08em, tabular numbers via font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums, B612 Mono for values/quantities and B612 (or Barlow Semi Condensed) for labels. Test whether B612 Mono has a slashed or dotted zero before relying on it (unverified).

Dotted leaders between the item label and its state (ECAM and QRH style) via a flex row with a flex:1 middle element using border-bottom: 1px dotted currentColor or a repeating radial-gradient. Treat as a style choice, since the search results did not confirm leaders on the real displays.

Bezel and box outlines: 1 to 2px solid white or cyan borders with square corners (border-radius 0 to 2px), an inset box-shadow for a screen-recess look, and a subtle CSS-only scanline or vignette via repeating-linear-gradient. Never rely on glow alone for state.

Pair every color with a non-color cue (check mark glyph, box fill vs outline, text such as REQUIRED) because green and red advisories are barred by the alerting rule and red/green confusion is common. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, replace any pulse/flash (Airbus amber pulse analogue) with a static thicker outline.

Use text-shadow: 0 0 4px color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 40%, transparent) at most, for a phosphor feel. Keep the shadow off when prefers-contrast: more or when the item is small, because glow smears thin B612 light-trap details.
